insider_note: 1/x sitting outside a function of logx is always the substitution trigger t=logx — dx/x becomes dt directly, with no extra algebra needed.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute t = logx
steps.why: The factor 1/x dx is EXACTLY dt once t=logx, since d/dx(logx)=1/x — the substitution removes x from the integral completely, leaving a plain function of t.
common_mistakes: Substituting t=logx but forgetting that dx alone (not dx/x) equals dt — it is the WHOLE 1/x dx that becomes dt.
Trying integration by parts instead of spotting the direct substitution.
steps.memory_tip: 1/x next to a function of logx ⇒ t=logx makes dx/x vanish into dt directly — no extra factor needed.

steps.label: Integrate and back-substitute for the final answer
steps.why: ∫sint dt = −cost + c is the most basic standard integral, and substituting t=logx back in returns the answer to the original variable x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to substitute logx back in for t in the final answer.
steps.memory_tip: ∫sint dt = −cost — sine integrates to NEGATIVE cosine, always.
